label: Submanifolds
notes: This chapter, printed pages 98 through 124, asks when a subset of a smooth manifold inherits its own smooth structure. We separate the well-behaved embedded case from the looser immersed case, then deploy the regular level set theorem as our main machine for producing examples.

label: Embedded Submanifolds
notes: An embedded submanifold carries the subspace topology and a smooth structure that makes the inclusion a smooth embedding. Stress both halves: the local model must look like a coordinate slice, and the topology must be inherited from the ambient space. Codimension is the number of constrained coordinates.

label: The Local Slice Condition
notes: The slice criterion is the local normal form for embedded submanifolds. In a suitable ambient chart the subset is exactly the points whose last n minus k coordinates equal constants. Emphasize that producing one such chart at every point is equivalent to being an embedded submanifold.

label: Regular Level Set Theorem
notes: Here is the chapter's workhorse. If c is a regular value of a smooth map F, then the level set is an embedded submanifold of codimension equal to the dimension of the target. Regularity means the differential is surjective at every preimage point, supplying the slice coordinates automatically.

label: Tangent Space is the Kernel
notes: At a point of a regular level set the tangent space is precisely the kernel of the differential of the defining map. Walk through both inclusions: curve velocities tangent to the level set are annihilated by dF, and dimension counting forces equality. The gradient is the visible normal direction.

label: The Sphere as a Level Set
notes: The unit sphere is the cleanest example: it is the level set of the squared norm at value one, and the differential is twice the position vector, never zero on the sphere. So one is a regular value and the sphere is an embedded hypersurface whose tangent plane is the orthogonal complement of the radius.

label: Matrix Group Examples
notes: The same theorem builds Lie groups. The special linear group is a regular level set of the determinant at one, and the orthogonal group is the level set of the map sending A to A transpose times A at the identity, landing in symmetric matrices. Count dimensions to confirm the codimensions.

label: Immersed Submanifolds
notes: An immersed submanifold relaxes the topology requirement: the inclusion is only an injective immersion, so the subset may carry a topology finer than the subspace one. The figure-eight image of a line is the standard cautionary tale, where the self-crossing point breaks the subspace topology.

label: Embedded vs Immersed
notes: Contrast the two side by side. Local rank behaviour is identical, so both are locally graphs, but global topology separates them. A graph is embedded; a singular zero set fails the rank test; a figure-eight has full rank yet the wrong topology at the crossing. Local data alone cannot certify embedding.

label: Tangent Space to a Submanifold
notes: Once the inclusion is fixed we view the tangent space of S as a linear subspace of the ambient tangent space, via the injective differential of the inclusion. For a level set this subspace is the kernel of the defining differential. Three viewpoints agree: curve velocity, gradient-orthogonality, and annihilator of vanishing functions.

label: Restricting Maps
notes: Restricting the domain of a smooth map to a submanifold is automatic: just compose with the inclusion. Restricting the codomain is subtler. A map into an immersed submanifold must also be continuous for the finer topology. Embedded and weakly embedded submanifolds pass this gate automatically for every smooth ambient map.

label: Submanifolds with Boundary
notes: At boundary points the local model is a half-slice rather than a full slice. A regular domain is the codimension-zero case with boundary, like the closed disk. A boundary defining function classifies directions by sign: positive points inward, negative outward, and zero stays tangent to the boundary.

label: Recap and the Rank-Drop Test
notes: Recap the logic chain and end with the lab. In the family x squared minus y squared minus epsilon, the gradient vanishes only at the origin, which sits on the zero level exactly when epsilon is zero. At that single parameter the curve crosses itself and stops being an embedded submanifold. Always check regularity first.
